title: The Family Care Map: Who Can Help, With What, and When?
subtitle: A flexible, one-page way to make caregiving offers, limits and next steps visible—without assuming that family members have already agreed to a role.
imageAlt: Three generations of a family seated around a kitchen table, looking together at a simple handwritten caregiving plan.
imageConcept: A warm, lived-in kitchen scene: an older adult, a middle-aged relative and a younger family member sit around a table with a blank one-page map, pens and cups of tea. The older adult is pointing to a note while the others listen; the paper is the focus, not a medical setting.
body: Care is easier to discuss before the emergency

A family may know that someone needs more help without knowing what “help” should look like. One person may be quietly handling appointments; another assumes a sibling is available for errands; the person receiving support may want company, not a new schedule. Those gaps can turn good intentions into confusion or resentment.

A family care map is a simple written record of what support is wanted, what people freely offer, what they cannot take on, and what needs another source of help. It is not a contract or a verdict on who cares most. It is a working page that can change as circumstances do. Guidance from the National Institute on Aging recommends talking with the older person and other helpers when there is no emergency, matching tasks to people’s skills and interests, and revisiting arrangements as needs and availability change [1].
Start with the person receiving support

Invite the person who may receive care to shape the conversation from the beginning. Ask what parts of everyday life are going well, where help would be welcome, and what they would prefer to keep doing themselves. Open questions leave room for an answer that is more precise than “I’m fine” or “I need help with everything”: “Which part of getting to appointments is hardest?” or “Would you like help with groceries, or would you rather we shop together?”

The answer may not be what relatives expect. A person might want a ride but not someone managing their calendar; they may welcome help with heavy chores while choosing their own meals and social plans. Record their preferences in their own words where possible. A person-centered approach puts values, goals and choices at the center, and treats a written support plan as something to update—not a one-time decision [2].

Choose a calm time and a manageable topic. If the person does not want to discuss every need at once, begin with one practical question and leave the rest for later. If they prefer not to participate in a particular conversation, respect that and clarify what they do want shared.
Name the tasks before assigning them

Write down the specific help that is being considered. Broad labels such as “handle Dad’s care” hide a dozen different tasks and make it hard to see what is actually needed. A more useful list might include: drive to a Tuesday appointment, pick up groceries once a week, check in by phone on Sunday, help compare home-service options, or spend an afternoon together while the usual caregiver takes a break.

For each item, note whether the help is wanted, how often it comes up, and whether it is time-sensitive. Separate tasks the person wants family to do from tasks that may call for a clinician, paid service or community organization. If no one knows how to handle a task safely, mark it as a question to investigate rather than assigning it to the most available relative.

This step also reveals that “being helpful” can mean different things. One person may be comfortable with paperwork but unable to drive; another may have time for a weekly visit but not urgent calls during work. Specifics make those differences useful rather than personal.

Give each person space to say what they can offer, what they cannot, and what conditions would make an offer workable. Try prompts such as: “I can take the Thursday appointment twice a month,” “I can help find a ride service, but I can’t be the regular driver,” or “I’m not available for overnight care.” A clear limit is information the group can plan around, not proof of indifference.

Avoid turning a family discussion into a vote on who should do more. The person who lives closest, has the most flexible schedule or is already doing the work may have constraints that others cannot see. Ask before adding a responsibility, and do not treat silence or a past favor as consent to an ongoing role. Caregiving guidance recommends matching responsibilities to people’s abilities and interests and sharing tasks clearly [1].

Put names beside only those tasks people have actually accepted. Include the scope and frequency: “Maya will call the ride service for next month’s appointment” is clearer than “Maya handles transportation.” If an offer depends on a changing schedule, write that down too.
Build in backup and outside support

A workable map does not depend on one person being endlessly available. For each essential task, ask what happens if the named helper is sick, away or no longer able to continue. The backup may be another relative, a friend who has agreed to help, a community resource, or a professional service—not necessarily another family member.

The map can name a next step even when no solution is settled: “Ask the clinic social worker about transportation options,” “Call the local aging office,” or “Find out whether a nearby adult day center offers respite.” The National Institute on Aging describes respite care as short-term relief that may take place at home, in a health care facility or at an adult day center [3]. The point is not to assume that a particular service is available, but to make finding out part of the plan.

Keep privacy in view when the discussion turns to health information. A family member should not assume they can receive medical details simply because they are helping.
Put the agreement on one page

Use a sheet of paper or a shared document with four simple headings: “Help wanted,” “Offers and limits,” “Backup or outside help,” and “Review date.” Under each task, record who agreed to do what and when. Add unresolved questions and the person who will follow up. Keep the language plain enough that someone who missed the conversation can understand the arrangement without interpreting family shorthand.

Before you finish, read the page back together. Ask the person receiving support whether it reflects what they asked for, and ask each helper whether their offers are written accurately. Correct any line that sounds more certain or more permanent than intended. If a decision affects someone’s private information, access or daily choices, clarify who has agreed to what rather than letting the document imply permission.

Keep the map somewhere appropriate and accessible to the people who need it. A shared file may work for one family; another may prefer a paper copy. Avoid putting sensitive details in a place or account that others can access without permission.
Revisit it when real life changes

Set a date to review the map, then bring it back sooner if a need, schedule or willingness changes. A plan that once worked may stop fitting after a move, a new health concern, a change in work hours or a helper’s own caregiving responsibilities. The purpose of a review is not to defend the old arrangement; it is to see whether the current one still reflects what the person wants and what others can genuinely do.

Use a few direct questions: What has been useful? What has become difficult? Is there anything on the page that no longer feels accurate? What support is missing? If the discussion gets tense, return to a specific task and the person’s stated preference rather than debating who is more committed. 

If the family cannot agree, record the difference rather than pretending it is settled. The next step might be a separate conversation, advice from a social worker or another relevant professional, or simply more time to consider the options.
Leave the map with one honest next move

For a first attempt, choose one ordinary, specific need—not every worry about the future. Perhaps the person receiving support wants help getting to a recurring appointment. Write down what they want, ask each person what they can freely offer, and name one backup or outside option if the first plan falls through. Put a date beside the next review, even if it is only a few weeks away.

Before leaving the table, let each person check the line that includes them. Is the offer accurate? Is the limit clear? Does the person receiving support recognize their own preference in the plan? If one answer is no, change the page now. A useful family care map is not the one that makes everyone look capable; it is the one that can be read honestly, adjusted without blame, and used to decide the next step together.
